 NPL final tickets sell out in seconds. Was it craze or embezzlement, fans question
 CAN and eSewa officials say the matter resulted from a large number of users accessing the app. They rule out black marketing. A number of fans had reached the TU International Cricket Stadium on Friday to protest the instantaneous sellout of the tickets for the final match.  Hemanta Shrestha/TKP bookmark facebook 
 twitter 
 Whatsapp 
 mail 
 Nayak Paudel 
 Published at : November 21, 2026 Updated at : November 21, 2026 08:13 Kirtipur The tickets for the final match of the third season of the Nepal Premier League were supposed to go live at 1pm Friday. Within seconds, they were sold out. Some even say that the tickets were reported ‘sold out’ even before the scheduled time for the sales to go live.  
 Nepali fans did not buy it.  
 eSewa, the ticketing platform for the third season, had prepared a system where one user could buy a maximum of five tickets. It takes at least a few seconds to go to the NPL section in the eSewa app, select the number of tickets and the section of the grandstands, and then proceed with payment. But the tickets were sold out as soon as they came live.  
 There was no end to speculations: someone hacked and bought tickets, eSewa did it purposely to sell the tickets in black, and the Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) supported eSewa.  
 To find the answers, which did not come to questions on the social media platforms of eSewa and CAN, the fans had reached the main gate of the TU International Cricket Stadium within an hour.  
 There were dozens of motorcycles parked along the road leading to the Tribhuvan University. Around 50 fans had heated arguments with police personnel, who stood between the protestors and the gate, when the Post reached the ground at around 2:30pm for a press meet with the captains of Lumbini Lions and Sudurpaschim Royals.  
 The conference, which was supposed to begin at 4:30pm, started only at 5:40pm. But there was one extra face in the captains’ pre-final press conference—Dhirendra Sawad, tournament director of the NPL.  
 Sawad was seated between Rohit Kumar Paudel and Dipendra Singh Airee. He was there to respond to the questions regarding the tickets’ issue—around an hour after CAN issued a statement. 
 “Around 200,000 users tried to buy tickets at once causing ‘concurrent requests’,” the statement read. “But we want to inform that the tickets were sold out within a few minutes as the stadium has a limited capacity.” 
 eSewa shared the same post by CAN on its social media.  
 Elaborating it after the captains had their say, Sawad said there were hundreds of thousands of users waiting to buy the tickets.  
 Sawad stressed the stadium’s seating capacity for 10,000. No tickets are sold for the stands on the Chobhar end, which can seat 2,000. For the TU-side stands, which have a capacity of 8,000, around 6,000 tickets are sold. 
 “But what we are confident about is that there was no black marketing,” he added. 
 By the time the press conference ended, the main gate was clean as the protesters had left. One thing was clear: they hadn’t got the tickets, nor a reasonable answer. 
 eSewa Chief Executive Officer Niraj Sharma told the Post that the last ticket was sold 24 minutes after sales opened at 1pm. As soon as sales went live, the system recorded concurrent purchase requests from around 200,000 users, resulting in technical difficulties. 
 “The system worked on a first-come, first-served basis,” Sharma said. “It is natural for spectators to be frustrated because only a small number of people managed to get tickets while most were unable to. But it was quite difficult for us to explain and manage the situation. We also coordinated with CAN, which issued an official statement.” 
 Nayak Paudel 
 Nayak Paudel covers sports for The Kathmandu Post. He previously worked at the Post (2018–19) and spent over five years at The Rising Nepal. His reporting spans crime, health, education, and social issues.
